table.text: We piloted the main study with 18 children to affirm that all vignettes were understandable and age-appropriate, and to estimate the session's duration for payment. Based on this pilot, we made minor changes to vignette wording and content, including removing two suspensemaximization vignettes that were too similar to the hidden present and sex of sibling vignettes and revising the prior experience measure. Because pilot measures differed from the final versions, we did not include the data in the main results (see Pilot study in the Supplementary materials; the main findings remain stable). Pilot data also confirmed that most children found the vignettes' characters (see Fig. 1) equally likable (72% indicated no preference for either at the end of a pilot session). Given limited prior evidence available at the time, we also used this pilot study to estimate the expected odds ratio for our main effect of interest, that is the effect of age on children's preference for deliberate ignorance, which indicated a small effect (OR ≈ 1.17). Simulation-based power analyses using this estimate indicated that a sample size of N = 150 children would allow us to detect even a small age effect with 80% power.

table.title: When children choose not to know
table.data_collection_started: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
Main question: How do children’s preferences for deliberate ignorance vary with age, and how are they associated with informational, developmental, and contextual factors?

Primary hypotheses:
Q1: Does a preference for deliberate ignorance exist in childhood?
H1: Deliberate ignorance exists in childhood. 

Q2: How is children’s preference for deliberate ignorance associated with age?
H2: Children’s preference for deliberate ignorance is positively associated with age, such that older children prefer deliberate ignorance more frequently than younger children. 

Q3: How is children’s preference for deliberate ignorance associated with the perceived existential threat of the information?
H3: Children’s deliberate ignorance varies with the perceived existential threat of the information presented in the scenario. 

Secondary hypotheses: 
Q4: How is children’s preference for deliberate ignorance associated with their ability to think about the future? 
H4: Children’s preference for deliberate ignorance is positively associated with their future-thinking ability, such that children with higher future-thinking abilities are more likely to prefer deliberate ignorance.

Q5: How is children’s preference for deliberate ignorance associated with their autonomy? 
H5: Children’s preference for deliberate ignorance is positively associated with their autonomy, such that more autonomous children are more likely to prefer deliberate ignorance. 

Q6: How is children’s preference for deliberate ignorance associated with their prior experience with the scenario content?
H6: Children’s preference for deliberate ignorance is positively associated with their prior experience with the scenario content, such that children with prior experience with a scenario content are more likely to prefer deliberate ignorance for the respective scenario.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Deliberate ignorance (binary): In each scenario (see below), children are shown two characters—one who prefers to know the information and one who prefers to remain ignorant—and asked to indicate who they would rather be. The child’s choice serves as a proxy for their own preference: 
Deliberate ignorance (1): Choose the character who does not want to know..
No deliberate ignorance (0): Choose the character who wants to know.

Example: Would you rather be like character A and find out what’s inside the hidden present, or like character B and not find out what’s inside the hidden present?
table.study_design_overview:
In this design, there is no assignment per se; all participants will be presented with the same 13 scenarios in randomized order.

Scenarios were designed to differ in the extent to which the information might pose an existential threat to the child, that is, whether they could seriously put their sense of safety or personal well-being at risk. To determine this on an individual level, children will rate the expected outcome of each scenario on a 5-point pictorial Likert scale from “very negative” to “very positive”. Those rated “very negative” will be categorized as “existential threat”, all others as “non-existential threat”.

Scenarios further vary in the types of emotions they involve and in what not knowing might help achieve—in some scenarios, ignorance may allow children to reduce negative emotion (e.g., fear, disgust, disappointment), while in others, it may allow them to increase positive emotion (e.g., surprise).
table.statistical_tests:
To address our research questions, we will fit a series of Bayesian logistic regression models using the R package brms to predict the key DV, deliberate ignorance. The DV will be modeled as a Bernoulli variable with a logit link function. Each model will include a random intercept for each child (1|id) to account for repeated observations. 

Q1 & Q2 → Model 1: Age 
This model will estimate the association between children’s preference for deliberate ignorance and their age. The intercept represents the average level of deliberate ignorance at the sample’s mean age. 

deliberate_ignorance ~ age + (1|id)

Q3 → Model 2: Perceived existential threat
This model will estimate the association between children’s preference for deliberate ignorance and the perceived existential threat of the information presented in the scenario (child-rated; 1 = existential; 0 = non-existential). 

deliberate_ignorance ~ existential_threat + (1|id)

Q4 → Model 3: Future-thinking ability
This model will estimate the association between children’s preference for deliberate ignorance and their future-thinking ability. Future-thinking ability is measured by the parent-reported mean score on the Episodic Foresight subscale of the Children’s Future-Thinking Questionnaire (CFTQ).

deliberate_ignorance ~ future_thinking + (1|id)

Q5 → Model 4: Autonomy 
This model will estimate the association between children’s preference for deliberate ignorance and their autonomy. Autonomy is measured by the parent-reported composite mean score of three items assessing autonomy in behavior, decision-making, and information selection. 

deliberate_ignorance ~ autonomy + (1|id)

Q6 → Model 5: Prior experience 
This model will estimate the association between children’s preference for deliberate ignorance and their prior experience with the scenario content (parent-reported; 1 = experience, 0 = no experience).

deliberate_ignorance ~ prior_experience + (1|id)

In separate regressions, we will control for children’s gender, parents’ education, socioeconomic status, and – if applicable – household (if more than one child participated from the same family).

We will assume weakly informative Cauchy priors for each regression coefficient: Cauchy(1, 0, 0.18). We will calculate Bayes factors (BF) to quantify the strength of evidence. BF > 3 will be taken as evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis; BF < ⅓ as evidence in favor of the null hypothesis. A BF greater than ⅓, but less than 3 will be treated as inconclusive. Posterior distributions and 95% credible intervals will be reported for all estimated effects.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participants will be fully excluded if:
They fail the initial comprehension check after the second attempt. 
Technical issues disrupt the session to the extent that participants’ responses are rated as uninterpretable by the experimenter. 
The experimenter judged the child’s choices as meaningless (e.g., due to heavy distraction, low motivation). 

Individual trials will be excluded if: 
Parents influence their decision in the given trial. 
The child explicitly states confusion or provides responses inconsistent with the scenario, indicating a lack of understanding.
table.sample_size: We aim to recruit 150 children aged 6 to 12 years, with a balanced distribution across gender (male/female) and age groups (6–7, 8–10, 11–12 years). Given limited prior evidence, we relied on pilot data to estimate the expected odds ratio for the effect of age on children's preference for deliberate ignorance, which indicated a small effect (OR ≈ 1.17). Simulation-based power analyses indicated that a sample size of N=150 children would allow us to detect a small age effect with 80% power. This target sample size represents a balance between maximizing statistical power within the financial and logistical constraints of recruiting a developmental sample.
table.additional_comments:
Given limited evidence of children’s deliberate ignorance, we include the following set of exploratory analyses to further examine how this preference may relate to the following additional factors: 

Scenario type: Two scenarios (hidden present, sex of sibling) are qualitatively distinct in that they involve open outcomes (e.g., present’s content) and target the suspense/surprise maximization function of deliberate ignorance. Although expected to fall under the non-existential category, we will run an exploratory analysis where we include them as a separate predictor level alongside existential and non-existential.

Existential threat: While the main analysis focuses on children’s perception of the scenario as existentially threatening, we will additionally explore parents’ and researchers’ classification of the scenarios. For reference, we (the researchers) designate the following scenarios as existential: parent fight, no money, moving house, robbery, parent illness, and parent lying; and the following as non-existential: missing out, sex of a sibling, hidden present, report card, broken toy, lottery, and maggot muesli. 

We will explore correlations between these different threat measures and fit model 2 using these as alternative predictors to assess consistency. 

Reported deliberate ignorance: Parents’ open-text reports of their children’s deliberate ignorance will be coded as existential/non-existential to further explore whether this distinction is reflected in parents’ real-life observations of deliberate ignorance. 

Motives for deliberate ignorance: Children’s explanations for a choice not to know will be coded for coherence with the scenario content and the type of explanation.

Parent-child alignment: We will explore the relationship between children’s preference for deliberate ignorance and 1) their parents’ predictions of their child’s deliberate ignorance (1 = deliberate ignorance, 0 = no deliberate ignorance), 2) their parents’ own preference for their child’s deliberate ignorance (categorical variable with three options, later collapsed into a binary variable; 0 = prefer them to know, 1 = prefer them not to know). 

Personality traits and curiosity: We will explore correlations between children’s preference for deliberate ignorance and their Big-Five personality traits (BFI-KJ-F), and curiosity (I/D-type curiosity scale).

Existing data: 
A pilot study (N=18) was conducted to check feasibility, data quality, and study design. To save resources, we will include pilot participants in the main analyses. Following the pilot, we made the following adjustments: 1) one scenario (hidden present) was reworded to better reflect the open-ended nature of the outcome, 2) the questions on parent-reported predictions, preferences, and prior experiences were revised to show each scenario exactly as shown to children rather than giving the overall topic, and 3) curiosity scale and parents’ threat rating were added. To ensure pilot data does not bias the results, all main analyses will be run with and without these pilot participants, and any differences will be reported. For 1), we will additionally conduct scenario-level comparisons; for 3), we will include only main study participants in the exploratory analyses.

text.text: When you were a child, did you tear open presents immediately or wait to savor the surprise?
When you heard your parents' loud voices, did you eavesdrop or retreat, trying not to hear?
These everyday moments reflect an important capacity: the ability to decide not to know, even when information is available, potentially relevant, and nearly costless.
This phenomenon has been called deliberate ignorance.
While deliberate ignorance is welldocumented in adults, including in highly consequential domains, such as health or social decisions, little is known about how it develops.
Across 13 vignettes we examined preferences for deliberate ignorance in 150 children aged 6 to 12 years.
We find that deliberate ignorance exists, already in middle childhood: On average, children preferred deliberate ignorance in 31% of cases; reaching up to 75% in one vignette.
Only 8% of children (n = 12) preferred to know across all vignettes.
Children with prior real-world experience with the presented information were more likely to prefer not to know, and this preference for deliberate ignorance increased with age.
Children preferred ignorance less for outcomes that they perceived as threatening.

Our findings offer new insights into early signatures of deliberate ignorance as a tool children use to regulate their information intake as they adapt to increasingly complex information environments with age.
The development of deliberate ignorance Children are often described as highly curious information-seekers who actively construct knowledge by interacting with their environment (Piaget, 1972).
text.formatted: The development of deliberate ignorance Children are often described as highly curious information-seekers who actively construct knowledge by interacting with their environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Piaget, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: Their behavior has been compared to that of scientists: from early on, they gather evidence efficiently and selectively (Ruggeri & Lombrozo, 2015); they seek explanations (Liquin & Lombrozo, 2020), construct theories, test hypotheses (Gopnik et al., 2017), and revise them (Gopnik & Wellman, 2012).
text.formatted: Their behavior has been compared to that of scientists: from early on, they gather evidence efficiently and selectively <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Ruggeri & Lombrozo, 2015)</ref>; they seek explanations <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Liquin & Lombrozo, 2020)</ref>, construct theories, test hypotheses <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Gopnik et al., 2017)</ref>, and revise them <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Gopnik & Wellman, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: They become increasingly aware of their own knowledge gaps (Molinaro et al., 2023; Ruggeri et al., 2024) and seek information to fill them.
text.formatted: They become increasingly aware of their own knowledge gaps <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Molinaro et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Ruggeri et al., 2024)</ref> and seek information to fill them.

text.text: To do so, they use their knowledge about how useful different sources will be for that (Harris et al., 2018; Koenig & Sabbagh, 2013); they integrate an answer's likely valence, instrumental value, and, increasingly, its potential to reduce their uncertainty (Molinaro et al., 2023).
text.formatted: To do so, they use their knowledge about how useful different sources will be for that <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Harris et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Koenig & Sabbagh, 2013)</ref>; they integrate an answer's likely valence, instrumental value, and, increasingly, its potential to reduce their uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Molinaro et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: But sometimes, children actively tame their thirst for information.
Consider the familiar image of a child, covering their ears to avoid hearing their parents' quarrel.

Here, the child does not use the opportunity to learn about the world (e.g., about the stability of their parents' relationship or relationships in general), prioritizing instead the goal to regulate their own emotions, including anxiety.
But when and why do they learn to do this?

Despite a growing theoretical literature on its development (Bonalumi & Ruggeri, 2025; Kerbl et al., 2025; Santhanagopalan et al., 2025b), few empirical studies have tested this perhaps strictest form of selectivity, that is "deliberate ignorance" (Hertwig & Engel, 2016), in childhood.
text.formatted: Despite a growing theoretical literature on its development <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bonalumi & Ruggeri, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kerbl et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Santhanagopalan et al., 2025b)</ref>, few empirical studies have tested this perhaps strictest form of selectivity, that is "deliberate ignorance" <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hertwig & Engel, 2016)</ref>, in childhood.

text.text: Deliberate ignorance is defined as the conscious choice not to learn information, even when it is available, nearly costless to acquire, and potentially personally relevant or beneficial (Hertwig & Engel, 2016).
text.formatted: Deliberate ignorance is defined as the conscious choice not to learn information, even when it is available, nearly costless to acquire, and potentially personally relevant or beneficial <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hertwig & Engel, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In this way, deliberate ignorance, though closely related to information avoidance, is more narrowly defined, excluding decisions not to know that result from inattention or forgetting, and cases in which information is avoided because the unwanted content is already known.

The closest concept is that of active information avoidance (Golman et al., 2017; Sweeny et al., 2010), yet we focus on deliberate ignorance as a dual-purpose mental tool, emphasizing both its intentional nature and the potential downsides as well as the sometimes adaptive nature of decisions not to know.
text.formatted: The closest concept is that of active information avoidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Golman et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Sweeny et al., 2010</ref>), yet we focus on deliberate ignorance as a dual-purpose mental tool, emphasizing both its intentional nature and the potential downsides as well as the sometimes adaptive nature of decisions not to know.

text.text: Deliberate ignorance is well-documented in adults, including in highly consequential domains such as for health, financial, dietary, climate, or social information (Gigerenzer & Garcia-Retamero, 2017; Hertwig et al., 2021; Ho, 2021; Reisch et al., 2021; Yang & Kahlor, 2013).
text.formatted: Deliberate ignorance is well-documented in adults, including in highly consequential domains such as for health, financial, dietary, climate, or social information <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gigerenzer & Garcia-Retamero, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hertwig et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Ho, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Reisch et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Yang & Kahlor, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Choosing not to know serves several functions, including to protect from negative emotions, such as regret, to preserve positive ones (e.g., savoring a surprise), secure strategic advantages, or manage limited cognitive resources (Hertwig & Engel, 2016).
text.formatted: Choosing not to know serves several functions, including to protect from negative emotions, such as regret, to preserve positive ones (e.g., savoring a surprise), secure strategic advantages, or manage limited cognitive resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hertwig & Engel, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Several explanations have been proposed as to how people arrive at a decision not to know.
Most prominently, the regret theory of deliberate ignorance describes it as a heuristic process (Gigerenzer & Garcia-Retamero, 2017), where the anticipated regret of knowing drives the choice.
text.formatted: Most prominently, the regret theory of deliberate ignorance describes it as a heuristic process <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gigerenzer & Garcia-Retamero, 2017)</ref>, where the anticipated regret of knowing drives the choice.

text.text: People consider the range of possible outcomes of knowing, identify the outcome with the most significant impact, and choose not to know if that outcome is negative.

Others instead describe it as a weighing process of the information's attributes, whereby its instrumental and affective value and its potential to reduce uncertainty are integrated to form a decision not to know (Sharot & Sunstein, 2020).
text.formatted: Others instead describe it as a weighing process of the information's attributes, whereby its instrumental and affective value and its potential to reduce uncertainty are integrated to form a decision not to know <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Sharot & Sunstein, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Both explanations, however, share that any decision not to know requires people to anticipate some consequences of knowing, or not knowing, information.
From a developmental perspective, deliberate ignorance should therefore emerge only once a child can foresee the benefits and drawbacks of having certain information.

This results in three levels to consider in any study of its development: Within the child, their ability to engage in future-thinking and simulating potential outcomes; within the information, the valence and magnitude of the outcomes at stake; within the environment, the conditions that make the functions laid out by Hertwig and Engel (2016) matter in the first place.
text.formatted: This results in three levels to consider in any study of its development: Within the child, their ability to engage in future-thinking and simulating potential outcomes; within the information, the valence and magnitude of the outcomes at stake; within the environment, the conditions that make the functions laid out by <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hertwig and Engel (2016)</ref> matter in the first place.

text.text: As long as parents still curate their children's environment, deliberate ignorance may not be a necessary response.

However, when this curation declines and children's access to information grows with their autonomy, the ability to decide what to ignore becomes an increasingly important cognitive tool (Kerbl et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, when this curation declines and children's access to information grows with their autonomy, the ability to decide what to ignore becomes an increasingly important cognitive tool <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kerbl et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We have previously argued that the choice to remain ignorant marks an important shift toward a more deliberate way of engaging with information and that its emergence, therefore, can offer insights into broader cognitive and environmental changes throughout development (Kerbl et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We have previously argued that the choice to remain ignorant marks an important shift toward a more deliberate way of engaging with information and that its emergence, therefore, can offer insights into broader cognitive and environmental changes throughout development <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kerbl et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The limited evidence available is consistent with a positive age trend (Santhanagopalan et al., 2025a): 5-to 6-year-old children show little sign of considering emotional stakes in their choices to seek or avoid information.
text.formatted: The limited evidence available is consistent with a positive age trend <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Santhanagopalan et al., 2025a)</ref>: 5-to 6-year-old children show little sign of considering emotional stakes in their choices to seek or avoid information.

text.text: But 7-to 8-yearolds avoid information more when it presents a threat (e.g., to emotions, self, or beliefs); this selective avoidance increases with age (Santhanagopalan et al., 2025a).
text.formatted: But 7-to 8-yearolds avoid information more when it presents a threat (e.g., to emotions, self, or beliefs); this selective avoidance increases with age <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Santhanagopalan et al., 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, evidence suggests that, although ignoring information was rare in children overall, when young children avoided information, they did so to benefit others (Brocas & Carrillo, 2020).
text.formatted: Furthermore, evidence suggests that, although ignoring information was rare in children overall, when young children avoided information, they did so to benefit others <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Brocas & Carrillo, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Both studies, however, used information with limited personal consequences (e.g., winning a prize, a party invite).
Neither tested higher-stakes or more threatening information, nor ignorance to maximize suspense, two cases that are prominent in the adult literature.
Furthermore, neither explored individual-level variables beyond age, or environmental factors that could help explain for whom and for which information deliberate ignorance emerges.
What, then, determines when and for what information children come to use this tool?
We test candidate predictors across three levels: within the child, within their environment, and within the information itself.
Within the child, deliberating whether to know or not requires them to foresee how a given type of information is likely to make them feel or act.
We hypothesize that this ability depends, in part, on direct or indirect experience with information and its consequences (Suddendorf, 2017).
text.formatted: We hypothesize that this ability depends, in part, on direct or indirect experience with information and its consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Suddendorf, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: A child who has already faced a comparable situation may have learned the emotional or practical costs of that information and can draw on this knowledge when faced with similar information.
Applying this past experience, however, requires projecting it into the future and anticipating the potential emotional and practical consequences of a new, similar situation.

This capacity develops throughout childhood (Atance, 2015), with the ability to anticipate more complex, counterfactual emotions -such as regret -emerging only later in childhood (McCormack & Feeney, 2015).
text.formatted: This capacity develops throughout childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Atance, 2015)</ref>, with the ability to anticipate more complex, counterfactual emotions -such as regret -emerging only later in childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(McCormack & Feeney, 2015</ref>).

text.text: Children's information environments also change with age.
As parental curation decreases, children become more autonomous in their information search; their social circles expand (Manalel & Antonucci, 2022).
text.formatted: As parental curation decreases, children become more autonomous in their information search; their social circles expand <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Manalel & Antonucci, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This growing independence and information access increases the occasions on which children must make their own decisions about information, allowing them to gather the relevant experience to direct their informational decisions.

Parental buffers that once curated information on their behalf are removed, making it increasingly important for children to decide for themselves what to engage with and what to ignore (Kerbl et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Parental buffers that once curated information on their behalf are removed, making it increasingly important for children to decide for themselves what to engage with and what to ignore <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kerbl et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: and what is likely at stake.

Adults exercise deliberate ignorance across life domains, but even when stakes are high, such as when avoiding consequential health information (Offer et al., 2025) or shunning information about their friends' and families' betrayal and lack of trustworthiness (Hertwig & Ellerbrock, 2022).
text.formatted: Adults exercise deliberate ignorance across life domains, but even when stakes are high, such as when avoiding consequential health information <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Offer et al., 2025)</ref> or shunning information about their friends' and families' betrayal and lack of trustworthiness <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hertwig & Ellerbrock, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This is also evident in the related "protective ignorance" where not knowing is discussed as a shield against threatening or uncontrollable events as one of its most consequential functions, for instance when sidestepping the result of a genetic test (Yaniv et al., 2004).
text.formatted: This is also evident in the related "protective ignorance" where not knowing is discussed as a shield against threatening or uncontrollable events as one of its most consequential functions, for instance when sidestepping the result of a genetic test <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Yaniv et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, deliberate ignorance may arise across a spectrum of perceived informational threats: from threats to a child's sense of safety, stability, and well-being (e.g., learning that a parent is severely ill), through unpleasant but less threatening discoveries (e.g., learning that one has eaten a maggot), to information that would merely disrupt an enjoyable mental state (e.g., ending the pleasurable suspense of not knowing what a wrapped present contains).
The present study examined preferences for deliberate ignorance in 6-to 12-yearolds (N = 150).
Across 13 vignettes, children indicated whether they would prefer to know certain information or not.

Moving beyond prior vignette-based work in adults and children (Hertwig et al., 2021; Santhanagopalan et al., 2025a), we included a wide range of vignettes with varying stakes, including threatening information where not knowing could help protect the child's sense of safety and personal well-being.
text.formatted: Moving beyond prior vignette-based work in adults and children <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hertwig et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Santhanagopalan et al., 2025a)</ref>, we included a wide range of vignettes with varying stakes, including threatening information where not knowing could help protect the child's sense of safety and personal well-being.

text.text: In addition to age, we tested predictors at each of the levels described: experience and future-thinking within the child, autonomy and caregiver preferences in the child's environment, and the stakes of the information itself -as potential explanations for when and for whom deliberate ignorance emerges across development.

It is also the first study that included a more qualitative approach to children's deliberate ignorance by asking children openly for their reasons for deliberate ignorance as well as collecting caregivers' reports of children's real-life choices to remain deliberately ignorant.
With this qualitative data we hope to provide additional, if exploratory information on the emergence of this phenomenon and a foothold for future work.

text.text: Participants were recruited through the Max Planck Institute for Human Development's (MPIB) participant database, 'Castellum' (Mader & Kleemeyer, 2023).
text.formatted: Participants were recruited through the Max Planck Institute for Human Development's (MPIB) participant database, 'Castellum' <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Mader & Kleemeyer, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the MPIB.
A parent or legal guardian provided written informed consent before their participation and that of their child.
Additionally, each child was asked to give verbal consent at the beginning of the session.
If they did not wish to participate at any point, the session was terminated.
There were no dropouts during any of the Zoom sessions.
Data collection took place from May 2024 to June 2026.
All sessions were conducted exclusively online via Zoom.
Families received 13 EUR for taking part in the study, compensating for both the caregiver questionnaire and child experimental session.
Our final sample included N = 150 children from 6 to 12 years old (M = 9.36 years, SD = 2.02, 76 girls, 74 boys). 10% of participants attended kindergarten; 90% attended primary school.
All children were native German speakers and were predominantly residents of Berlin, so most children in our sample are likely growing up in an urban environment.

Families were from predominantly higher-socioeconomic and educated backgrounds: 81% of caregivers reported holding a university degree (reported for one caregiver); 64% reported a net annual household income above 63.000 EUR, a level reached by roughly one in six German households.
We tested 152 children in total.

However, two caregivers did not complete the parent survey, so we recruited two additional child-caregiver dyads to reach our target sample and excluded the two children without caregiver-reported data.
No other children or individual trials were excluded; all children passed the comprehension checks, and no sessions were affected by technical issues or inattention as judged by the experimenter.
Due to a technical error, open-ended responses for two children were not available for coding (26 reasons).
We piloted the main study with 18 children to affirm that all vignettes were understandable and age-appropriate, and to estimate the session's duration for payment.

Based on this pilot, we made minor changes to vignette wording and content, including removing two suspensemaximization vignettes that were too similar to the hidden present and sex of sibling vignettes and revising the prior experience measure.
Because pilot measures differed from the final versions, we did not include the data in the main results (see Pilot study in the Supplementary materials; the main findings remain stable).
Pilot data also confirmed that most children found the vignettes' characters (see Fig. 1) equally likable (72% indicated no preference for either at the end of a pilot session).

Simulation-based power analyses using this estimate indicated that a sample size of N = 150 children would allow us to detect even a small age effect with 80% power.
Children participated in an experimenter-moderated study via Zoom.
An experimenter greeted the child and caregiver on Zoom and asked for the children's verbal consent.
If they agreed, the experimenter began by introducing the children to two characters, Fiz and Fip (Figure 1), who would make decisions about finding out information or not.

text.text: We opted for this third-person framing because we wanted to ask about more sensitive information, including potentially threatening information.
We did not want to ask children to imagine their own parents getting sick or quarreling.

This method was inspired by the Berkeley Puppet Interview (Measelle et al., 1998), where an experimenter typically introduces two characters which state opposing views (e.g., "I'm shy when I meet new people." or "I'm not shy when I meet new people" Measelle et al., 2005).

It also helped to even participants' understanding of the situation and kept the cues concrete and relatable (e.g., an empty fridge, a hidden present), making the vignettes easy to imagine and engaging rather than asking to reason about abstract preferences.
The location (left/right) and informational preferences of the characters were randomized across vignettes and between participants.

For each vignette, children were asked to answer three questions (Figure 1E): Q1) Which character they would rather be like -the one who finds out or the one who does not find out (main DV: deliberate ignorance; binary response); Q2) Why the one character who did not want to know would prefer this (open response); Q3) How they think the characters would feel if the information turned out to be true (5-point pictorial Likert scale).

text.text: The latter measure is intended to gauge the participant's perceived extent of the threat.

After completing all 13 vignettes, children were asked whether they preferred one character over the other and whether they, like the characters, could think of something that they would prefer not to know.
The entire session lasted approximately 30 minutes.

All vignettes were adapted from comparable situations used in adult deliberate ignorance paradigms (Hertwig et al., 2021) and modified in content, language and complexity to be age-appropriate for children.

text.text: We piloted the vignettes with caregivers of children aged 6 to 12 via Prolific (N = 38), asking them to predict whether their child would want to know the information in each vignette.
This provided preliminary evidence that the vignettes were relevant and meaningful to children and that we could expect some variation in children's epistemic preferences in this age range.
The content of all vignettes is presented in Table S1.
text.formatted: The content of all vignettes is presented in Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>.

text.text: The vignettes covered a range of situations with varying stakes.
They primarily targeted the emotion-regulation function of deliberate ignorance, yet across a range of possible emotions (e.g., disgust, fear, disappointment).
Two vignettes targeted the suspense maximization function of deliberate ignorance (hidden present and sex of sibling).
Vignettes also varied in whether the anticipated outcome might threaten the child's sense of safety and personal well-being.

We included this variation because many of the adult cases that preceded this work are highly threatening (e.g., not wanting to know about a medical test result, Stasi files, or one's date of death) and we wanted a comprehensive account of how an informational threat would relate to children's deliberate ignorance.

Because this is the first attempt at classifying information along this dimension in this age range, we therefore did not want to rely on a single judgement, but chose to include three sources -the child's, their caregiver's, and the researchers'.
Each vignette was classified a priori by the research team as extreme threat or not based on whether the anticipated outcome would threaten the child's sense of safety and personal well-being.
The classification is noted in the preregistration.

Parent fight, no money, move, robbery, sick parent, and parent lied were registered as extreme threat; sick self, sex of sibling, hidden present, report card, broken toy, lottery, and maggot muesli as no extreme threat.
Note that we used "existential" vs. "non-existential" in the preregistration but adopted "extreme" vs.
"non-extreme" to better describe also the child's proxy.
To determine perceived threat on an individual level, children rated the expected outcome of each vignette on a 5-point pictorial Likert scale (see Q3 in Fig. 1E).
text.formatted: To determine perceived threat on an individual level, children rated the expected outcome of each vignette on a 5-point pictorial Likert scale (see Q3 in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1E</ref>).

text.text: We classified only ratings of 5 (the most negative) as "extreme threat", all others as "non-extreme threat".
Finally, caregivers rated each vignette in terms of whether they thought their child would perceive it as threatening (see Table S2).

text.text: Before the child's Zoom session, caregivers completed an online questionnaire.
For each vignette, caregivers answered four questions: 1) "Would your child want to know this information?"
(yes/no); 2) "Would your child consider this information as a serious threat to their own safety and well-being?"
(rather threatening/rather not threatening); 3) "Would you want your child to know this information?"

(yes/no/no and would actively prevent); 4) "To the best of your knowledge, has your child previously encountered a similar situation or topic, either directly (through personal experience) or indirectly (e.g., through friends, stories, or school materials)?"
(yes/no).
An open-ended question further asked caregivers to recount real-world observations in which their child had actively chosen not to know something.
We then classified these examples as extreme threat or not.

In addition, caregivers completed standardized questionnaires pertaining to their child's personality (Big Five Inventory for children and adolescents, other-rated (Kupper et al., 2021), trait curiosity (Litman & Mussel, 2013; Piotrowski et al., 2014), and future-thinking (Episodic Foresight subscale of the Children's Future-Thinking Questionnaire (CFTQ); Mazachowsky & Mahy, 2020).

text.text: Autonomy was assessed via three items on behavioral, decision, and information autonomy.
The first two were adapted from Neubauer et al. (2021) and we added the third to assess the extent to which children decide independently which information they engage with.

text.text: We fitted a series of Bayesian logistic regression models using the 'brms' package (Bürkner, 2017) in R (R Core Team, 2022).
text.formatted: We fitted a series of Bayesian logistic regression models using the 'brms' package <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bürkner, 2017)</ref> in R (R Core Team, 2022).

text.text: We modeled the dependent variable, whether children preferred deliberate ignorance (coded as 1) or not (coded as 0), as a Bernoulli variable with a logit link.
Because each child answered 13 vignettes, we included a random intercept for each child to account for repeated observations.

The main pre-registered predictors were age (in months; standardized), perceived threat of the information (0 = non-extreme,1 = extreme), future-thinking ability (caregiverreported mean score on the Episodic Foresight subscale of the CFTQ; standardized), autonomy (caregiver-reported composite score of three items assessing behavioral, decision, and informational autonomy; standardized), and caregiver-reported prior experience with the vignette content (0 = no experience,1 = experience).
In line with our preregistration, we fitted separate models for each predictor.
In additional models, we included children's gender and caregiver education as covariates (see Table S3 (with covariates) and Table S4, Model 2).
text.formatted: In additional models, we included children's gender and caregiver education as covariates (see Table <ref type="table">S3</ref> (with covariates) and Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>, Model 2).

text.text: Socioeconomic status (SES; measured as net annual household income) and household were also preregistered as a covariate and a random effect, respectively.
However, we did not include SES because it was highly skewed, nor household, because the small number of sibling pairs (14 pairs; 28 participants) produced divergent transitions.
Because few caregivers did not hold a university degree, we binarized caregiver education (university degree, including doctorate, vs. no university degree).
In an exploratory analysis, we fitted a separate model including all main predictors to explore their contribution while controlling for the others (see Table S4).
text.formatted: In an exploratory analysis, we fitted a separate model including all main predictors to explore their contribution while controlling for the others (see Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: To rule out multicollinearity, we examined correlations among predictors.
These were negligible to moderate.
Age was moderately correlated with future-thinking (r = 0.38) and weakly to moderately with autonomy (r = 0.26).
Future-thinking and autonomy were also weakly to moderately correlated (r = 0.26).

Age and prior experience were not correlated (see Table S5), which we primarily attribute to the limited age range and selection of vignettes where experience might not primarily accumulate by age (see Discussion).

text.text: We specified weakly informative Cauchy priors with central tendency 0 and dispersion of 0.18 for each regression coefficient.
Posterior distributions were summarized using posterior medians and 95% credible intervals.

To quantify evidence for each predictor, we computed Bayes factors (BF) for regression coefficients using the Savage-Dickey density ratio method (Wagenmakers et al., 2010) and the 'bayestestR' package (Makowski et al., 2019).

text.text: Across all 13 vignettes, children preferred not to know 31% of the time.
Twelve children (8%) chose to know on all 13 vignettes.
Descriptively, children in the youngest age group (6-7 years) showed lower rates of deliberate ignorance (24%) than those in the middle (8-10 years; 32%) and oldest age group (11-12 years; 37%).
Girls preferred not to know in 31% of choices; boys in 30%.
Preferences for deliberate ignorance varied greatly across vignettes: Most children preferred not to know about the contents of a hidden present (75%).
Among the remaining vignettes, deliberate ignorance was most common for parent fight (44%), maggot muesli (43%), and lottery (39%).
Rates were lowest for move (17%) and sick self (17%).

Of the 1,924 reasons available for coding, 84% (n = 1,617) contained a coherent reason.

We defined coherent reasons broadly as any interpretable explanation of why the deliberately ignorant character might not want to know, excluding no answer, "don't know", and nonsensical or off-topic responses.

Out of those reasons, 61% contained an emotional reason, 25% cognitive, 16% instrumental, 4% irrelevant (note that 104 contained two reason types, so the percentages add up to more than 100), showing that the vignettes worked well in targeting the emotional regulatory function of deliberate ignorance.

The low rate of "irrelevant" ratings further shows that deliberate ignorance here was not because of a lack of interest and that we captured deliberate ignorance in its strict form, where information is ignored even though it is personally relevant (see Fig. S1).

So far, researchers have primarily used hypothetical vignettes to study deliberate ignorance in children and adults, with the information chosen and framed by the researchers.

To complement this approach, we also asked caregivers directly whether they had ever observed their children deliberately choosing not to know in real life, and, if so, to describe up to three instances.
They did so after rating the vignettes (see Method).
These findings are exploratory.
Our main goal here was to collect first real-life instances of deliberate ignorance in childhood to inform future work.
Roughly half of the caregivers (n = 74) reported that they had observed at least one instance of deliberate ignorance with their children.
In total, caregivers provided 165 opentext examples of deliberate ignorance in their children's everyday life.

All except one of these caregivers described at least one such example in more detail; 87% (n = 144) of which could be coded as deliberate ignorance in line with the definition as "a deliberate choice not to know even when the information is available and potentially of personal relevance or benefit" (Hertwig & Engel, 2016). 10% (n = 17) did not meet the definition and described a situation where the child was uninterested (e.g., a "boring explanation during a museum tour", age 11).

text.text: The remaining four examples were too brief to be reliably coded as an example of deliberate ignorance or not.

We then coded whether the information was an extreme threat; that is, whether knowing it could seriously threaten the child's sense of safety and personal well-being, including threats to the child or their immediate environment.

Among deliberate ignorance examples, 24% (n = 34) were coded as extreme threats: Caregivers reported children not wanting to know how seriously ill their grandfather was (age 12, male) or how a TV show about the Holocaust and the persecution of Jewish people ended (age 7, male). 76% were coded as no extreme threat and ranged from not wanting to know information about sex (age 8, female) to a child who "asked once or twice if we [the parents] are actually St.
Nicholas leaving something outside the door at night, but he was easily satisfied by a little white lie that it's not us.
Since then, he hasn't asked or tried to prove it anymore.
Of course, he's not threatened by this but just enjoys the story and the small presents each year" (age 11, male).
Finally, we coded the motive for deliberate ignorance using the framework proposed by Hertwig and Engel (2016).
text.formatted: Finally, we coded the motive for deliberate ignorance using the framework proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hertwig and Engel (2016)</ref>.

text.text: Most examples were coded as emotion regulation (44%, n = 63) or suspense maximization (19%, n = 28); 30% (n = 43) were too brief to code a motive (see Fig. S2).

text.text: We investigated if and under what circumstances children, who are usually described as curious information-seekers, prefer to remain deliberately ignorant and decide not to know easily available and potentially relevant information.
We found clear evidence for the existence of the preference for deliberate ignorance in middle childhood, across a broader range of vignettes than previously tested.
Deliberate ignorance was present already at six years old and became more common with age.

This fits within the broader view of children as selective information-seekers who are better able to integrate multiple aspects of information, such as its valence, instrumental value, and uncertainty as they get older (Molinaro et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This fits within the broader view of children as selective information-seekers who are better able to integrate multiple aspects of information, such as its valence, instrumental value, and uncertainty as they get older <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Molinaro et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The strongest individual-level predictor of deliberate ignorance next to age was experience.

Children with prior experience of a situation were considerably more likely to prefer not to know its outcome, and this effect held after accounting for age; age and experience were not correlated (see below).
This suggests that the development of deliberate ignorance is more strongly related to individual experiences than to more general measures of cognitive maturation.

In other words, deliberate ignorance seems like an experience-dependent developmental outcome that children develop in adaptive response to their environment, rather than an experience-expectant outcome that every child will develop on a common timetable given only exposure to ubiquitous and prototypical inputs, irrespective of idiosyncratic life experiences (Greenough et al., 1987).
text.formatted: In other words, deliberate ignorance seems like an experience-dependent developmental outcome that children develop in adaptive response to their environment, rather than an experience-expectant outcome that every child will develop on a common timetable given only exposure to ubiquitous and prototypical inputs, irrespective of idiosyncratic life experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Greenough et al., 1987)</ref>.

text.text: The age trend we found aligns with Santhanagopalan et al. (2025a), who found that the youngest children in their study (5 to 6-year-olds) avoided information mainly when explicitly told to prioritize feeling happy over learning; anticipating benefits of not knowing without this prompt became more common only in the older age groups.
text.formatted: The age trend we found aligns with <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Santhanagopalan et al. (2025a)</ref>, who found that the youngest children in their study (5 to 6-year-olds) avoided information mainly when explicitly told to prioritize feeling happy over learning; anticipating benefits of not knowing without this prompt became more common only in the older age groups.

text.text: We find the same age trend under a different setup.
Instead of instructing children which goal to pursue, we named the unwanted outcome -other than for the two suspense-maximization vignettesso that the stakes were given, but the goal was not.
What varied with age was whether children translated those stakes into a choice not to know.

Irrespective of their own choice, most young children in our sample were able to give us reasons for decisions not to want to know for a given vignette (from 66% of 6-year-olds), suggesting they understood the benefit of deliberate ignorance even though they acted on it less so themselves.
This understanding became even more common with age (for comparison, 92% in 12-year-olds gave coherent reasons).
Age and prior experience were uncorrelated in our sample, which was surprising.

We had expected experience to increase with age, because of environmental changes, but also simply because more time makes it more likely that probabilistic events will occur (Ciranka & Hertwig, 2023).
text.formatted: We had expected experience to increase with age, because of environmental changes, but also simply because more time makes it more likely that probabilistic events will occur <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Ciranka & Hertwig, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: One reason for this may be that the vignettes' situations differ in when they might occur across childhood.
Some have a clear developmental starting point and accumulate near linearly, as when children enter school and are confronted with grades year after year.
Others are determined by the specifics of the child's proximate environment and household (Bronfenbrenner, 1979) and therefore occur irrespective of age.
text.formatted: Others are determined by the specifics of the child's proximate environment and household <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bronfenbrenner, 1979)</ref> and therefore occur irrespective of age.

text.text: Examples include whether caregivers show conflict openly, whether illness or scarcity are present, and which topics are spoken about at all.
Still others depend on events in the broader environment and thus differ between cohorts.
For instance, children who lived through the COVID-19 pandemic encountered information about serious illness and death more frequently than children growing up a decade earlier (Dalton et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For instance, children who lived through the COVID-19 pandemic encountered information about serious illness and death more frequently than children growing up a decade earlier <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dalton et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Such effects can mask a linear accumulation of experience with age.
Our measurement of prior experience may have further contributed to that because we asked for a binary report, including indirect experiences.
This breadth may apply early to more children, masking direct experience that accumulates with age.
On the information level, deliberate ignorance was less common for vignettes whose outcomes children rated as more threatening.
This pattern held whether threat was rated by children or classified a priori by the research team and was inconclusive for caregiver-rated threat (see Table S6).
text.formatted: This pattern held whether threat was rated by children or classified a priori by the research team and was inconclusive for caregiver-rated threat (see Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>).

text.text: One possible explanation comes from work on children's explanationseeking curiosity, which suggests that unexpected information or expectation-violation reliably motivates children to seek out more information (Liquin & Lombrozo, 2020).
text.formatted: One possible explanation comes from work on children's explanationseeking curiosity, which suggests that unexpected information or expectation-violation reliably motivates children to seek out more information <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Liquin & Lombrozo, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: If the more threatening vignettes tended to violate children's expectations more strongly (e.g., the expectation that their parent is always healthy), this could explain why children were drawn more towards such information.
A second explanation could be differences in actionability.
With age, children increasingly consider the instrumental value of information (Molinaro et al., 2023).
text.formatted: With age, children increasingly consider the instrumental value of information <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Molinaro et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: If children perceive threatening vignettes as more actionable, this could further explain their preference to know.

These are only two possible factors that may override an overarching and age-independent preference for positive information (Molinaro et al., 2023), which on its own would predict ignoring rather than learning threatening information.
text.formatted: These are only two possible factors that may override an overarching and age-independent preference for positive information <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Molinaro et al., 2023)</ref>, which on its own would predict ignoring rather than learning threatening information.

text.text: That a wish to evade an extreme threat can nonetheless underlie deliberate ignorance outside the laboratory is suggested by caregivers' open-ended real-world examples of children's deliberate ignorance, roughly a quarter of which involved extremely threatening information.
Within the child, future-thinking ability as measured by the CFTQ was not associated with children's preference for deliberate ignorance.
This was also unexpected as the ability to deliberate about the future outcome of a decision is fundamental to the development of deliberate ignorance (Kerbl et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This was also unexpected as the ability to deliberate about the future outcome of a decision is fundamental to the development of deliberate ignorance <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kerbl et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: One likely explanation for this lack of association lies in the scope of the items included in the CFTQ Episodic Foresight subscale (Mazachowsky & Mahy, 2020).
text.formatted: One likely explanation for this lack of association lies in the scope of the items included in the CFTQ Episodic Foresight subscale <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Mazachowsky & Mahy, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Most of its items assess children's ability to anticipate future physiological and practical states (e.g., feeling hungry or needing a jacket).
They are only somewhat relevant to the present vignettes that heavily focus on emotional content.
Deliberate ignorance in our study likely relies more on affective future-thinking, i.e., the ability to anticipate future emotional responses to information (see e.g., (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005).
text.formatted: Deliberate ignorance in our study likely relies more on affective future-thinking, i.e., the ability to anticipate future emotional responses to information (see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Wilson & Gilbert, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: This was also reflected in the qualitative reasons reported above, which were not only coherent but overwhelmingly affective in nature as opposed to instrumental or cognitive.
Together this suggests that most children were already able to effectively forecast emotional states.
Similarly surprising, we found no association between children's preference for deliberate ignorance and autonomy over their behavior, decisions, and information.

We included autonomy as a candidate environmental influence on deliberate ignorance, given that the degree to which information is managed for children changes with age and affects their exposure to information.
As children become more autonomous, they have more occasion to practice to regulate their information intake, which we hypothesized would lead to more deliberate ignorance.
Children's autonomy did increase with age, as expected, but this did not relate to differences in deliberate ignorance.

One reason may be that the children we tested are likely still transitioning toward autonomy and experience it in other realms (Ke, 2023), such as deciding which things to spend their time with or what they like to eat.
text.formatted: One reason may be that the children we tested are likely still transitioning toward autonomy and experience it in other realms <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Ke, 2023)</ref>, such as deciding which things to spend their time with or what they like to eat.

text.text: Only the transition from adolescence to young adulthood grants people legal autonomy (Steinberg, 2013) over most consequential life decisions.
text.formatted: Only the transition from adolescence to young adulthood grants people legal autonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Steinberg, 2013)</ref> over most consequential life decisions.

text.text: Another is that autonomy is not the only route to managing information.
Some children are shielded from threatening information by those around them, while others handle it themselves early on.
Children who are protected by other means may have little occasion or need to protect themselves.
Consistent with this, children were more likely to prefer not to know when their caregiver preferred that for them.

Caregiver preference is another path through which the environment takes effect: children learn not only from what happens to them, but from how people around them, especially parents, approach information (Luce et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Caregiver preference is another path through which the environment takes effect: children learn not only from what happens to them, but from how people around them, especially parents, approach information <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Luce et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Caregivers may model their own ignorance in everyday interactions, much as their explanation-and exploration behaviors are influenced by parents' prompts and encouragement (Legare et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Caregivers may model their own ignorance in everyday interactions, much as their explanation-and exploration behaviors are influenced by parents' prompts and encouragement <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Legare et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: They may also signal more explicitly through the norms they teach around certain topics, for instance, that you should not eavesdrop on people's conversations, no matter how relevant (Tam, 2015), or their beliefs about what children should or should not know (e.g., about death, sexuality, or world news).
text.formatted: They may also signal more explicitly through the norms they teach around certain topics, for instance, that you should not eavesdrop on people's conversations, no matter how relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Tam, 2015)</ref>, or their beliefs about what children should or should not know (e.g., about death, sexuality, or world news).

text.text: Deliberate ignorance in childhood may thus be shaped less by general autonomy than by what the immediate environment signals about specific contents.
What children experience, including their caregivers' preferences, are features of the environment children grow up in.
This implies that the experiences that make deliberate ignorance adaptive are clustered within social groups.

Adverse childhood experiences have been argued to shape information-seeking behavior (Frankenhuis & Gopnik, 2023), and lower-SES households tend to experience more illness, conflict, and scarcity of resources (Ciranka et al., 2026; Merrick et al., 2018), all of which were presented in our vignettes.
text.formatted: Adverse childhood experiences have been argued to shape information-seeking behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Frankenhuis & Gopnik, 2023)</ref>, and lower-SES households tend to experience more illness, conflict, and scarcity of resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Ciranka et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Merrick et al., 2018)</ref>, all of which were presented in our vignettes.

text.text: Because nearly two-thirds of our sample reported household incomes above 63.000 EUR per year -a level reached by roughly one in six German households -it remains an open question how this pattern would look in a more economically diverse sample, where informational experiences might differ.
For instance, if the prior experience effect holds, a more diverse sample would likely have reported a higher proportion of choices not to know in our set of vignettes.
Future studies should look at how both differ between groups: which situations children encounter in the first place and how their caregivers approach and teach information management.
First and foremost, this was a cross-sectional study, so we cannot speak to any age trends within individuals (Hamaker, 2023).
text.formatted: First and foremost, this was a cross-sectional study, so we cannot speak to any age trends within individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hamaker, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Confirming that the patterns we observed reflect developmental trajectories will require longitudinal data, particularly given the wide variability we found between children and vignettes.

Future studies should also extend beyond the 6 to 12 age range: to younger children, to pinpoint its first emergence, and to adolescents, to explore how preferences and functions shift with children's priorities, for instance, to protect against social threats.
Our main design limitation concerns the vignettes.
We prioritized exploring a wide range of vignettes and tested 13 vignettes across stakes and emotions, but we did not experimentally manipulate them.

The framing highlighted the unwanted outcome, i.e., we asked, "whether the parents are seriously ill" rather than neutrally, "whether the parents are seriously ill or perfectly healthy", so that children across age groups had a similar and accessible understanding of the stakes.
This means we cannot say what rates of deliberate ignorance would look like under neutral or positive framing.

We also formulated all vignettes in the third person, which allowed us to ask about more sensitive topics while minimizing distress (with precedent in the Berkeley Puppet Interview; (Herzog et al., 2024; Measelle et al., 2005; Yee et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We also formulated all vignettes in the third person, which allowed us to ask about more sensitive topics while minimizing distress (with precedent in the Berkeley Puppet Interview; <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Herzog et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Measelle et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Yee et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: But imagining one's own family in distress would likely have a different effect.
We see some evidence of this in caregivers' reports of experienced deliberate ignorance in their child that concern distressing family-related information (e.g., the illness of a family member).

Finally, the vignettes' content carried norms and experiences of their own: Deliberate ignorance for less threatening outcomes was driven mainly by the hidden present vignette that three quarters of children had experiences with.
Deliberate ignorance preferences here are likely shaped by cultural norms encouraging not to peek at presents to savor the surprise.
However, the second surprise vignette -sex of siblingshowed markedly lower deliberate ignorance rates.

Earlier work with adults found a related cultural pattern: German and Spanish adults differed in their preference to remain ignorant of a Christmas present's contents and for learning an unborn child's sex (Gigerenzer & Garcia-Retamero, 2017).
text.formatted: Earlier work with adults found a related cultural pattern: German and Spanish adults differed in their preference to remain ignorant of a Christmas present's contents and for learning an unborn child's sex <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gigerenzer & Garcia-Retamero, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should move beyond functional categories to test such normative and cultural differences by manipulating them within vignettes.

Similarly, they could manipulate the target emotion (e.g., anxiety, disgust, regret) as well as informational dimensions such as actionability, whether information is delayed (as in present, sex of sibling) or irreversibly ignored (as in lottery).
Such a design would also allow a more rigorous test of the informational threat itself, which we could approximate here only through children's valence ratings.

What is extremely threatening to a child cannot be judged by an adult alone, yet asking directly would require prompting children to think about a threat to their own safety and personal well-being, which we considered unethical.

Varying a vignette's threat -for instance, its magnitude (e.g., a minor versus serious illness) or the social distance to the persons involved (e.g., a parent vs. an acquaintance) -would help determine whether the association between extreme or non-extreme threats and deliberate ignorance is mainly a matter of degree or a qualitatively different concern related to a sense of personal safety and well-being.
Finally, hypothetical vignettes do not capture the conditions under which children might truly avoid information in real life.
An important next step would therefore be to elicit children's actual choices in behavioral choice paradigms.

For instance, by giving children the option to reveal or ignore information about a forgone option, in studies of anticipated regret (Guttentag & Ferrell, 2008), or letting them gain real strategic benefits by remaining ignorant (Brocas & Carrillo, 2020; Santhanagopalan et al., 2025a).
text.formatted: For instance, by giving children the option to reveal or ignore information about a forgone option, in studies of anticipated regret <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Guttentag & Ferrell, 2008)</ref>, or letting them gain real strategic benefits by remaining ignorant <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Brocas & Carrillo, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Santhanagopalan et al., 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: A key sampling limitation regards representativeness.
As discussed above, our sample was predominantly high-SES and highly educated.
Prior experience and, more tentatively, caregiver preference are to some extent properties of the household that likely differ by SES.
Testing these patterns in socioeconomically and culturally diverse samples should be a priority in future studies.
Several of our measures, including prior experience, relied on a single caregiver's report (in 88% of cases, the mother).

In Germany, spend the most time with children and are thus best placed to report on their experiences (Walper & Kreyenfeld, 2022), but such reports are likely less accurate for older children who spend less time with their primary caregivers (Manalel & Antonucci, 2022).
text.formatted: In Germany, spend the most time with children and are thus best placed to report on their experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Walper & Kreyenfeld, 2022)</ref>, but such reports are likely less accurate for older children who spend less time with their primary caregivers <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Manalel & Antonucci, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: And because testing happened online, those same caregivers were often present while children answered, which may have shaped responses to the vignettes, especially when about caregivers.

Future studies should therefore aim to collect children's preferences without a caregiver present, as well as a direct and more in-depth assessment of their experience with information including its valence, frequency, and outcome.
Moving away from hypothetical setups, one could, for instance, imagine collecting children's experience with report cards in classrooms and their subsequent decisions to review or ignore feedback.
We coded children's reasons for coherence and general type (emotional, cognitive, instrumental) but did not analyze their content in depth as their brevity did not allow for substantial conclusions.
Future studies could explore reasons for deliberate ignorance in more depth, for instance by using LLM interview techniques (Skeggs et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Future studies could explore reasons for deliberate ignorance in more depth, for instance by using LLM interview techniques <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Skeggs et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Open questions include how the complexity of reasons changes with age, whether the types of emotions children report change (e.g., given that some emotions, like regret, develop later McCormack et al., 2020), how children's normative views on epistemic states develop over time and differ between families and cultures.
Similar techniques could be used to also ask children directly about their own real-world examples of deliberate ignorance to complement the caregiver reports.
From as early as six years old, children can identify benefits to not knowing and explicitly express preferences to do so.
They do so increasingly with accumulating experience and age.

Children's own reasons suggest that this is not only the absence of curiosity, but deliberate decisions that children inform through experience to manage increasingly complex, less externally curated, information.
Children's choices not to know thus provide an informative window into their cognitive development and the experiences they make.
Knowing what children do not want to know and why will help to foster the cognitive toolbox children need to meet the demands of evermore complex information environments.
Together, our results contribute to a growing body of work that illustrates the development of choices not to know across childhood.
